claims.claim: The other 245 dendrobatid species compose several other primarily inconspicuously colored clades that for the most part have been assumed to lack alkaloid defenses: Aromobatinae, Hyloxalinae, and some Colostethinae.
claims.source: The other 245 species compose several other primarily inconspicuously colored clades that for the most part have been assumed to lack alkaloid defenses: that is, all Aromobatinae (e.g. Allobates, Rheobates, Anomaloglossus, and Aromobates), all Hyloxalinae (Ectopoglossus, Hyloxalus, Paruwrobates), and some Colostethinae (Colostethus, Silverstoneia, Leucostethus; Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic knowledge and Figure 1.

claims.claim: According to the phylogenetic placement of defended and undefended species within Dendrobatidae, poison frogs have evolved sequestration of lipophilic alkaloids from consumed arthropods at least three times.
claims.source: According to the phylogenetic placement of defended and undefended species within Dendrobatidae, poison frogs have evolved sequestration of lipophilic alkaloids from consumed arthropods at least three times (Santos et al., 2014; Santos et al., 2003), making them a suitable group to study complex phenotypic transitions like the evolution of chemical defense.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Santos et al., 2014 and Santos et al., 2003.

claims.claim: The study surveyed 104 animals representing 32 species of Neotropical frogs including 28 dendrobatid species, 2 bufonids, 1 leptodactylid, and 1 eleutherodactylid.
claims.source: In total, we surveyed 104 animals representing 32 species of Neotropical frogs including 28 dendrobatid species, 2 bufonids, 1 leptodactylid, and 1 eleutherodactylid (see Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the study's sample size and composition.

claims.claim: Each of the major undefended clades in Dendrobatidae is represented in the dataset, with a total of 14 undefended dendrobatid species surveyed.
claims.source: Each of the major undefended clades in Dendrobatidae (Figure 1, Table 1) is represented in our dataset, with a total of 14 undefended dendrobatid species surveyed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Figure 1 and Table 1.

claims.claim: Both undefended and defended dendrobatid species consume a large proportion of ants and mites.
claims.source: Both undefended and defended dendrobatid species consume a large proportion of ants and mites (Figure 2; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by diet data shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Defended dendrobatid clades tend to consume proportionally more ants and mites than undefended lineages.
claims.source: Although the defended dendrobatid clades tend to consume proportionally more ants and mites, as in other studies, the undefended lineages do consume a high proportion of ants and mites.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from diet data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Ants and mites respectively constituted up to 51% and 60% of the stomach contents of the undefended dendrobatids Allobates talamancae and Hyloxalus sauli.
claims.source: Other data support this general pattern: ants and mites respectively constituted up to 51% and 60% of the stomach contents of the undefended dendrobatids Allobates talamancae (Mebs et al., 2018) and Hyloxalus sauli (Darst et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Mebs et al., 2018 and Darst et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Ants and mites compose nearly 50% of the arthropods (36% and 10%, respectively) found in the Silverstoneia flotator stomachs analyzed in this study.
claims.source: Ants and mites compose nearly 50% of the arthropods (36% and 10%, respectively) found in the Silverstoneia flotator stomachs we analyzed (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by diet data in Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Sympatric populations of the undefended Hyloxalus awa and defended Epipedobates espinosai are both diet specialized, with the former consuming mostly ants and beetles and the latter consuming mostly mites and springtails.
claims.source: Sympatric populations of the undefended Hyloxalus awa and defended Epipedobates espinosai (formerly E. darwinwallacei López-Hervas et al., 2024) are both diet specialized, with the former consuming mostly ants and beetles and the latter consuming mostly mites and springtails (Sánchez-Loja et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to López-Hervas et al., 2024 and Sánchez-Loja et al., 2024.

claims.claim: In a lab experiment, the defended species Dendrobates tinctorius preferred fruit fly larvae over ants when given the choice.
claims.source: In a lab experiment, the defended species Dendrobates tinctorius preferred fruit fly larvae over ants when given the choice (Moskowitz et al., 2022b), suggesting that even in defended species, consumption of possible alkaloid-containing prey is not necessarily a preference.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Moskowitz et al., 2022b.

claims.claim: Oophaga sylvatica alkaloid quantity is inversely correlated with numbers of consumed ants and mites.
claims.source: Another study revealed that Oophaga sylvatica alkaloid quantity is inversely correlated with numbers of consumed ants and mites; however, this species consumed more mites and ants than sympatric Hyloxalus elachyhistus (Moskowitz et al., 2022a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Moskowitz et al., 2022a.

claims.claim: If we assume that many ants and mites contain alkaloids, it is likely that most if not all dendrobatids and their most recent common ancestors have long been exposed to toxins through their diet.
claims.source: Thus, if we assume that many ants and mites contain alkaloids, it is likely that most if not all dendrobatids and their most recent common ancestors have long been exposed to toxins through their diet.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on diet data and knowledge about alkaloid sources.

claims.claim: Target-site resistance to some alkaloids evolved in several defended dendrobatid clades and in some undefended species.
claims.source: Indeed, target-site resistance to some alkaloids evolved in several defended dendrobatid clades and in some undefended species (Tarvin et al., 2017; Tarvin et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Tarvin et al., 2017 and Tarvin et al., 2016.

claims.claim: A few defended species have alternative target mechanisms including binding proteins like alpha-binding globulin and saxiphilin that might prevent alkaloids from accessing their molecular targets.
claims.source: A few defended species have alternative target mechanisms including binding proteins like alpha-binding globulin (Alvarez-Buylla et al., 2023) and saxiphilin (Abderemane-Ali et al., 2021) that might prevent alkaloids from accessing their molecular targets (e.g. ion channels).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Alvarez-Buylla et al., 2023 and Abderemane-Ali et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Poison frogs may biotransform alkaloids into less toxic forms until they can be eliminated from the body, for example using cytochrome p450s.
claims.source: For example, poison frogs may biotransform alkaloids into less toxic forms until they can be eliminated from the body, for example using cytochrome p450s (Caty et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Caty et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Only 31 of the 245 inconspicuous poison frog species described to date have been assessed for toxins.
claims.source: By reviewing existing data, we found that only 31 of the 245 inconspicuous poison frog species described to date AmphibiaWeb, 2023 have been assessed for toxins, sometimes using methods that would not necessarily detect lipophilic alkaloids (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on a review of prior studies documented in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: At least 11 undefended species might have lipophilic alkaloids: Allobates femoralis, Allobates kingsburyi, Allobates zaparo, Colostethus ucumari, H. elachyhistus, Hyloxalus nexipus, Hyloxalus vertebralis, Hyloxalus yasuni, Leucostethus fugax, Paruwrobates erythromos, and Silverstoneia punctiventris.
claims.source: Our review and reassessment of these studies suggest that at least 11 undefended species might have lipophilic alkaloids: Allobates femoralis, Allobates kingsburyi, Allobates zaparo, Colostethus ucumari, H. elachyhistus, Hyloxalus nexipus, Hyloxalus vertebralis, Hyloxalus yasuni, Leucostethus fugax, Paruwrobates erythromos, and Silverstoneia punctiventris (Daly et al., 1987; Darst et al., 2005; Gonzalez et al., 2021; Grant, 2007; Moskowitz et al., 2022a; Santos and Cannatella, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is based on a review of prior studies with citations to Daly et al., 1987; Darst et al., 2005; Gonzalez et al., 2021; Grant, 2007; Moskowitz et al., 2022a; and Santos and Cannatella, 2011.

claims.claim: Using GC-MS, the study surveyed 89 animals representing 30 species of Neotropical frogs including 27 dendrobatid species, 1 leptodactylid, and 2 bufonids.
claims.source: Using Gas-Chromatography Mass-Spectrometry (GC-MS), we surveyed 89 animals representing 30 species of Neotropical frogs including 27 dendrobatid species, 1 leptodactylid, and 2 bufonids (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the GC-MS sample set, supported by Figure 2.

claims.claim: The study performed a highly sensitive, untargeted analysis using UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS of a dendrobatid from an undefended clade (S. flotator; 12 individuals) and a species of eleutherodactylid (Eleutherodactylus cystignathoides; 3 individuals).
claims.source: We also performed a highly sensitive, untargeted analysis —ultra-high-performance liquid-chromatography heated-electrospray-ionization tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS) — of a dendrobatid from an undefended clade (S. flotator; 12 individuals) and a species of eleutherodactylid (Eleutherodactylus cystignathoides; 3 individuals), in which alkaloid diversities and types, but not quantities, were assessed.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS sample set.

claims.claim: Alkaloids were detected in skins from 13 of the 14 undefended dendrobatid species included in the study, although often with less diversity and relatively lower quantities than in defended lineages.
claims.source: Overall, we detected alkaloids in skins from 13 of the 14 undefended dendrobatid species included in our study, although often with less diversity and relatively lower quantities than in defended lineages (Figure 2, Table 1, Supplementary file 3, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 2, Table 1, and Supplementary files 3 and 4.

claims.claim: The pervasiveness of low alkaloid levels in undefended dendrobatid lineages contrasts with the mixed or opposing evidence from previous analyses.
claims.source: The pervasiveness of low alkaloid levels in undefended dendrobatid lineages (Aromobatinae, Hyloxalinae, some species of Colostethinae) contrasts with the mixed or opposing evidence from previous analyses (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of current data with prior studies documented in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: The GC-MS assessment revealed substantially higher diversities of alkaloids in defended dendrobatid species than previously reported.
claims.source: In addition, our GC-MS assessment revealed substantially higher diversities of alkaloids in defended dendrobatid species than previously reported (Cipriani and Rivera, 2009; Daly et al., 1987; Lawrence et al., 2023; Moskowitz et al., 2022a,), and expands knowledge on major classes of alkaloids within genera.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of current GC-MS data with prior studies cited.

claims.claim: Alkaloids were detected in all four Rheobates palmatus individuals sampled, with one individual having at least four classes of compounds represented.
claims.source: Alkaloids were detected in all four R. palmatus individuals sampled, with one individual having at least four classes of compounds represented (4,6-disubstituted quinolizidines, 3,5-disubstituted indolizidines, 3,5-disubstituted pyrrolizidines, and unclassified).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: Five species of Allobates all had detectable levels of alkaloids.
claims.source: We found that five species of Allobates all had detectable levels of alkaloids.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: Allobates insperatus had a relatively high level of alkaloid diversity, with at least 18 alkaloids from nine classes detected, and at least one class found in each of the eight sampled individuals.
claims.source: Allobates insperatus had a relatively high level of alkaloid diversity, with at least 18 alkaloids from nine classes detected, and at least one class found in each of the eight sampled individuals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: Only one unclassified alkaloid was identified in a single individual of Allobates juanii while two were found in one individual of Al. kingsburyi.
claims.source: In contrast, only one unclassified alkaloid was identified in a single individual of Al. juanii while two were found in one individual of Al. kingsburyi.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: At least two alkaloids were identified in each of the three sampled individuals of Allobates talamancae (including the lehmizidine 277 A and five new alkaloids).
claims.source: At least two alkaloids were identified in each of the three sampled individuals of Al. talamancae (including the lehmizidine 277 A and five new alkaloids).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: Eight alkaloids were identified in the single surveyed Allobates zaparo individual (including the spiropyrrolizidines 222–1 and 222–2 as well as six unclassified alkaloids).
claims.source: Eight alkaloids were identified in the single surveyed Al. zaparo individual (including the spiropyrrolizidines 222–1 and 222–2 as well as six unclassified alkaloids).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: Prior assessments using thin-layer chromatography suggested the presence of alkaloids in three Al. kingsburyi, but none in 12 Al. insperatus.
claims.source: Prior assessments using thin-layer chromatography suggested the presence of alkaloids in three Al. kingsburyi (Santos and Cannatella, 2011), but none in 12 Al. insperatus (Darst et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is based on citations to Santos and Cannatella, 2011 and Darst et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Four studies failed to identify any alkaloids in Al. talamancae.
claims.source: Four studies (Supplementary file 2) failed to identify any alkaloids in Al. talamancae.
claims.evidence: This is based on review of prior studies documented in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: Allobates zaparo was shown to possibly have trace alkaloids, although the interpretation of these data was absence of alkaloids.
claims.source: Allobates zaparo was shown to possibly have trace alkaloids, although the interpretation of these data was absence of alkaloids (Darst et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is based on citation to Darst et al., 2005.

claims.claim: From Leucostethus fugax, the study identified a total of twelve 5-substituted indolizidine, 5,6-disubstituted indolizidine, pyrrolidine, spiropyrrolizidine, and unclassified alkaloids, with three to eight unique compounds detected in each of the eight sampled individuals.
claims.source: From L. fugax, we identified a total of twelve 5-substituted indolizidine, 5,6-disubstituted indolizidine, pyrrolidine, spiropyrrolizidine, and unclassified alkaloids (196 A, 225 C, 222–1, 222–2, and eight new alkaloids), with three to eight unique compounds detected in each of the eight sampled individuals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: The study's data are consistent with prior thin-layer chromatography data showing that L. fugax tested positive for skin compounds.
claims.source: Our data are consistent with prior thin-layer chromatography data showing that L. fugax tested positive for skin compounds (Santos and Cannatella, 2011), although prior interpretations of these data were different (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with prior data from Santos and Cannatella, 2011.

claims.claim: Alkaloids were found in all nine Silverstoneia aff. gutturalis, with a total of 14 alkaloids identified across seven classes.
claims.source: We found alkaloids in all nine S. aff. gutturalis, with a total of 14 alkaloids identified across seven classes (196 A, 223I, 233 A, 235B, 237 U, three isomers of 239AB, two isomers of 239 CD, and four new alkaloids).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: In just two individuals of Silverstoneia erasmios, the study detected a total of 26 alkaloids, including some pumiliotoxins and pyrrolizidines.
claims.source: In just two individuals of S. erasmios, we detected a total of 26 alkaloids, including some pumiliotoxins (325B, 323B) and pyrrolizidines (225 C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: Thirteen alkaloids were found in eight individuals of Silverstoneia punctiventris.
claims.source: Silverstoneia erasmios and S. aff. gutturalis had not been surveyed for alkaloids previously, but thirteen alkaloids were found in eight individuals of a congener (S. punctiventris; Gonzalez et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is based on citation to Gonzalez et al., 2021.

claims.claim: In the UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS analysis of S. flotator, alkaloids were identified in 5 of 12 sampled individuals (a quinolizidine and epibatidine).
claims.source: In addition, in our more conservative UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS analysis of S. flotator, from which we only report compounds with formulae or from classes previously known for lipophilic alkaloids of frogs (Daly et al., 2005), we identified the presence of alkaloids in 5 of 12 sampled individuals (a quinolizidine and epibatidine; Supplementary file 5, Supplementary file 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS data in Supplementary files 5 and 6.

claims.claim: When the analysis was expanded to include any compound assigned to the 'alkaloid pathway' by NPClassifier, a total of 67 compounds were identified in S. flotator, some of which were present in each individual.
claims.source: When we expand our analysis to include any compound assigned to the 'alkaloid pathway' by NPClassifier (>99% alkaloid pathway probability; Supplementary file 5), we identified a total of 67 compounds, some of which were present in each individual (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS data in Supplementary file 5.

claims.claim: Most of the individual skins of Epipedobates and Ameerega contained dozens to more than one hundred unique alkaloids.
claims.source: In terms of the defended clades of Colostethinae that we sampled, most of the individual skins of Epipedobates and Ameerega contained dozens to more than one hundred unique alkaloids (see Supplementary file 4 for full details).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data in Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: For Ameerega, the study surveyed five individuals representing two species, all of which had integrated areas that were more than 75,000 x greater compared to individuals of its sister clade, Leucostethus.
claims.source: For Ameerega, we surveyed five individuals representing two species, all of which had integrated areas that were more than 75,000 x greater compared to individuals of its sister clade, Leucostethus (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data in Table 1.

claims.claim: Alkaloid diversity was 10–20 x greater in Ameerega than in Leucostethus.
claims.source: Similarly, alkaloid diversity was 10–20 x greater in Ameerega than in Leucostethus.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from GC-MS data.

claims.claim: Histrionicotoxins and decahydroquinolines were considered previously to be the dominant alkaloid classes in genus Ameerega; this study also found high levels of indolizidines.
claims.source: Histrionicotoxins and decahydroquinolines were considered previously to be the dominant alkaloid classes in genus Ameerega Daly et al., 2009; here we also found high levels of indolizidines (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of current data (Figure 2) with prior knowledge from Daly et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The study surveyed 13 individuals representing seven species in Epipedobates and identified at least 370 alkaloids.
claims.source: We surveyed 13 individuals representing seven species in Epipedobates and identified at least 370 alkaloids, which contrasts with studies using a less sensitive method (thin-layer chromatography) that found mixed evidence for the presence of alkaloids in E. aff. espinosai (then referred to as E. boulengeri) and E. machalilla (Darst et al., 2005; Santos and Cannatella, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data and comparison with prior studies cited.

claims.claim: The quantity and diversity of alkaloids in Epipedobates machalilla was substantially lower than in other Epipedobates species, occurring at levels similar to Silverstoneia spp.
claims.source: However, the quantity and diversity of alkaloids in Epipedobates machalilla was substantially lower than in other Epipedobates species, occurring at levels similar to Silverstoneia spp. (Table 1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claims.claim: Except for E. machalilla, each Epipedobates species had about 10 x greater quantities and diversities of alkaloids compared to members of Silverstoneia.
claims.source: Except for E. machalilla, each Epipedobates species had about 10 x greater quantities and diversities of alkaloids compared to members of Silverstoneia.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from GC-MS data.

claims.claim: The study found trace levels of epibatidine in Epipedobates anthonyi but not in other Epipedobates species.
claims.source: We found trace levels of epibatidine in Epipedobates anthonyi but not in other Epipedobates species.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: Epibatidines have been detected in E. espinosai, Ameerega silverstonei, S. flotator, and Ameerega petersi or a closely related, undescribed species.
claims.source: Epibatidines have also been detected in E. espinosai, Ameerega silverstonei, S. flotator (Daly et al., 1999; this study), and Ameerega petersi or a closely related, undescribed species (reported as Dendrobates pictus from Loreto, Peru in Daly et al., 1987, but see taxonomic revision by Guillory et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Daly et al., 1999; Daly et al., 1987; Guillory et al., 2020; and data from this study.

claims.claim: The study surveyed four species of Hyloxalus, three of which had detectable levels of alkaloids.
claims.source: We surveyed four species of Hyloxalus, three of which had detectable levels of alkaloids.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: The study identified 17 different alkaloids in H. awa, with the seven sampled individuals having 0–12 alkaloids each.
claims.source: We identified 17 different alkaloids in H. awa (197D, 197 H, 199B, 217B, 221 P, 223AB, 231 A, 231 C, 247E, and eight previously undescribed alkaloids), with the seven sampled individuals having 0–12 alkaloids each.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: The study detected five alkaloids in a single individual of H. shuar and eight alkaloids in a single individual of H. sp. Agua Azul.
claims.source: We detected five alkaloids in a single individual of H. shuar (197D, 199B, 237 G, and two isomers of 239 K) and eight alkaloids in a single individual of H. sp. Agua Azul (195 C, 197D, 199B, 251 K, and four new alkaloids).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: The detection of low levels of alkaloids in H. awa is consistent with the observations that avian predators consume H. awa.
claims.source: Our detection of low levels of alkaloids in H. awa is consistent with the observations that avian predators consume H. awa (Darst and Cummings, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is based on citation to Darst and Cummings, 2006.

claims.claim: No alkaloids were detected in two individuals of H. toachi, the only undefended dendrobatid species from which the study failed to detect alkaloids.
claims.source: No alkaloids were detected in two individuals of H. toachi, the only undefended dendrobatid species from which we failed to detect alkaloids.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: A GC-MS assessment revealed that Paruwrobates erythromos contained 5,8-disubstituted indolizidine 251B, allopumiliotoxin 267 A, and unclassified alkaloid 281D.
claims.source: Previously, a GC-MS assessment revealed that P. erythromos contained 5,8-disubstituted indolizidine 251B, allopumiliotoxin 267 A, and unclassified alkaloid 281D (Daly et al., 1987).
claims.evidence: This is based on citation to Daly et al., 1987.

claims.claim: Hyloxalus azureiventris is thought to be able to accumulate alkaloids.
claims.source: Hyloxalus azureiventris is also thought be able to accumulate alkaloids (Daly, 1998; Saporito et al., 2009)
claims.evidence: This is based on citations to Daly, 1998 and Saporito et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Thin-layer chromatography suggested the presence of alkaloids in two assessed H. yasuni, one of three H. nexipus, and two of five H. vertebralis.
claims.source: and thin-layer chromatography suggested the presence of alkaloids in two assessed H. yasuni (previously identified as Hyloxalus maculosus), one of three H. nexipus, and two of five H. vertebralis (Santos and Cannatella, 2011), although prior interpretation of these data differed (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on citation to Santos and Cannatella, 2011.

claims.claim: From Dendrobatinae, the study surveyed 18 individuals representing five species using GC-MS.
claims.source: From this subfamily, we surveyed 18 individuals representing five species using GC-MS.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the sample set.

claims.claim: The study identified a total of 187 unique alkaloids from four Phyllobates aurotaenia, 316 alkaloids from five O. sylvatica, and 213 alkaloids from three Dendrobates truncatus.
claims.source: We identified a total of 187 unique alkaloids from four Phyllobates aurotaenia, 316 alkaloids from five O. sylvatica, and 213 alkaloids from three Dendrobates truncatus.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: P. aurotaenia, O. sylvatica, and D. truncatus are all relatively large poison frogs (snout-vent lengths 20–35 mm), which may in part explain their high alkaloid diversities and quantities.
claims.source: These three species are all relatively large poison frogs (snout-vent lengths 20–35 mm; Supplementary file 3), which may in part explain their high alkaloid diversities and quantities (Jeckel et al., 2015; Saporito et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological data in Supplementary file 3 and citations to Jeckel et al., 2015 and Saporito et al., 2010.

claims.claim: In Andinobates minutus and Andinobates fulguritus, the study detected 129 and 109 alkaloids, respectively.
claims.source: In Andinobates minutus and Andinobates fulguritus, which are members of the same subfamily but are much smaller in size (11–15 mm; Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 3), we detected 129 and 109 alkaloids, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data and morphological data in Supplementary files 1 and 3.

claims.claim: The total alkaloid quantities (integrated areas) in D. truncatus and O. sylvatica were comparable to those of Ameerega but were higher than quantities detected in Epipedobates.
claims.source: The total alkaloid quantities (integrated areas) in D. truncatus and O. sylvatica were comparable to those of Ameerega but were higher than quantities detected in Epipedobates.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from GC-MS data.

claims.claim: The study reports for the first time the occurrence of N-methyldecahydroquinolines outside of the genera Adelphobates, Ameerega, Dendrobates, Oophaga, and Ranitomeya.
claims.source: We also report for the first time, to the best of our knowledge, the occurrence of N-methyldecahydroquinolines outside of the genera Adelphobates, Ameerega, Dendrobates, Oophaga, and Ranitomeya (in E. aff. espinosai, E. currulao, S. aff. gutturalis, An. minutus, An. fulguritus, P. aurotaenia, and Al. insperatus; Daly et al., 2009; Hovey et al., 2018; Jeckel et al., 2019; Lawrence et al., 2019; Stuckert et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data and comparison with prior studies cited.

claims.claim: The ability to N-methylate decahydroquinoline (demonstrated experimentally in Adelphobates galactonotus, Dendorbates auratus, and Ranitomeya ventrimaculata) may be conserved in dendrobatids, or arthropod sources of the alkaloid class (likely myrmicine ants) are widespread.
claims.source: The ability to N-methylate decahydroquinoline (demonstrated experimentally in Adelphobates galactonotus, Dendorbates auratus, and Ranitomeya ventrimaculata Jeckel, 2021; Jeckel et al., 2022) may thus be conserved in dendrobatids, or, non-exclusively, arthropod sources of the alkaloid class (likely myrmicine ants Jones et al., 1999) are widespread.
claims.evidence: This is based on citations to Jeckel, 2021; Jeckel et al., 2022; and Jones et al., 1999, combined with inference.

claims.claim: The study detected a new unclassified alkaloid, New159, in each of two A. siona (Bufonidae).
claims.source: Outside of Dendrobatidae, we detected a new unclassified alkaloid, New159, in each of two A. siona (Bufonidae)
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: The study detected four alkaloids in one individual of Atelopus aff. spurrelli (Bufonidae).
claims.source: and four alkaloids in one individual of Atelopus aff. spurrelli (Bufonidae; 3,5-disubstituted pyrrolizidine 237 R-1, decahydroquinoline 243 A-3, 5,8-disubstituted indolizidine 251B-2, and an unclassified alkaloid, New267-2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC-MS data.

claims.claim: The detection of a decahydroquinoline and a 3,5-disubstituted pyrrolizidine in a bufonid frog other than Melanophryniscus is novel.

claims.claim: Short-term alkaloid feeding experiments demonstrate that both defended and undefended frogs can survive the immediate effects of alkaloid intake, although the degree of resistance and the alkaloids that different species can resist vary.

claims.claim: An experiment showed that two aposematic dendrobatids (D. tinctorius and Phyllobates terribilis), an aposematic Mantella (Mantella aurantiaca), and the putatively undefended rhacophorid Polypedates leucomystax recovered from injections of the highly toxic alkaloids batrachotoxin and tetrodotoxin delivered at 20 x the mouse LD50 value.
claims.source: An experiment conducted by Abderemane-Ali et al., 2021 showed that both aposematic and (presumably) undefended frogs can withstand several highly toxic alkaloids in quantities greater than what the frogs are likely to experience in nature. Two aposematic dendrobatids (D. tinctorius and Phyllobates terribilis), an aposematic Mantella (Mantella aurantiaca), and the putatively undefended rhacophorid Polypedates leucomystax (a congener is reported to contain TTX Tanu et al., 2001) — recovered from injections of the highly toxic alkaloids batrachotoxin and tetrodotoxin delivered at 20 x the mouse LD50 value.

claims.claim: The three aposematic species (D. tinctorius, P. terribilis, and M. aurantiaca) also survived a third potent alkaloid (saxitoxin), but P. leucomystax did not.

claims.claim: Different types of resistance may be important during different evolutionary phases leading to chemical defense.

claims.claim: The ability to metabolize toxins can in some cases augment toxin defenses, increase the toxicity of a compound, or result in some amount of passive accumulation through increased toxin exposure.

results.result: Undefended dendrobatid species from multiple clades (Aromobatinae, Hyloxalinae, Colostethinae) contain measurable but low levels of alkaloids in their skin, contrasting with previous studies that found no alkaloids in these lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C50-C82 collectively demonstrate through GC-MS and UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS data that 13 of 14 undefended dendrobatid species surveyed contain detectable alkaloids, albeit at lower quantities and diversity than defended species. The data are presented in Table 1, Figure 2, and supplementary files, with specific alkaloid identifications for multiple species across different clades. This finding is robust and well-documented.

results.result: Both defended and undefended dendrobatid species consume substantial proportions of ants and mites (known alkaloid sources), with defended species consuming proportionally more but undefended species still showing high consumption rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C35-C42 are supported by diet analysis data in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1, showing that undefended species consume up to 51% ants and 60% mites. Multiple citations to prior studies (Mebs et al., 2018; Darst et al., 2005; Sánchez-Loja et al., 2024) corroborate these findings. The data consistently demonstrate overlap in diet composition between defended and undefended species.

results.result: Diet alone is insufficient to explain the defended phenotype in poison frogs; alkaloid accumulation results from multiple processes including toxin intake, elimination, and sequestration.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C104 are supported by the convergence of diet data (showing similar consumption patterns) and alkaloid data (showing vastly different accumulation levels) between defended and undefended species. The inference that diet is insufficient is logically sound given that both groups consume similar alkaloid-bearing prey yet differ dramatically in alkaloid accumulation (Table 1, Figure 2).

results.result: The authors propose a passive accumulation hypothesis defining an intermediate phenotype between toxin consumption and sequestration, characterized by low toxin elimination rates without derived transport/storage mechanisms, resulting in low-level toxin accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C25, C28-C29, C105-C107 present a coherent conceptual framework supported by the empirical data showing low alkaloid levels in undefended species. The hypothesis is grounded in pharmacokinetic principles (C23-C24) and provides a mechanistic explanation for the observed pattern. While speculative in mechanism, the phenotypic pattern it describes is well-documented in the data.

results.result: Both defended and undefended dendrobatid species exhibit alkaloid resistance, with experimental evidence showing survival after exposure to toxic alkaloids, though the degree and type of resistance varies among species.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44, C112-C119 are supported by multiple experimental studies (Tarvin et al., 2017, 2016; Abderemane-Ali et al., 2021; Jeckel, 2021; Waters et al., 2024) demonstrating that both defended and undefended frogs can survive alkaloid exposure. The data show variation in resistance mechanisms and effectiveness across species, supporting the claim that some level of resistance exists broadly in dendrobatids.

results.result: Experimental evidence demonstrates differential alkaloid elimination rates between defended and undefended species, with undefended species accumulating <1% of administered alkaloids while defended species sequester 10-50%, supporting the hypothesis that elimination rates differ between phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C137 are supported by experimental data from Jeckel (2021) and other studies showing quantitative differences in alkaloid uptake and elimination. The data consistently show that undefended species (Al. femoralis, Hy. cinerea) accumulate minimal alkaloids while defended species (Ad. galactonotus, D. tinctorius) sequester substantial amounts. This supports Prediction 2 of the passive-accumulation hypothesis.

results.result: Evidence suggests that sequestration mechanisms (e.g., alkaloid-binding proteins) are present in defended species but absent or minimally expressed in undefended species, with experimental feeding studies showing undefended species fail to accumulate alkaloids from prey.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C151 are supported by biochemical data (Alvarez-Buylla et al., 2023) showing binding protein activity in defended but not undefended species, and feeding experiments (Daly et al., 1994b; Jeckel, 2021; Sanchez et al., 2019) demonstrating differential uptake. The convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches supports the claim that sequestration mechanisms differ between defended and undefended lineages.

results.result: Poison frogs (Dendrobatidae) have evolved the ability to acquire alkaloids for chemical defense at least three times independently, with approximately 100 of 345 species in three defended clades and 245 species in undefended clades.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C30-C32 are supported by phylogenetic analyses (Santos et al., 2014, 2003) and taxonomic data (AmphibiaWeb, 2023). The phylogenetic placement of defended and undefended lineages clearly indicates multiple independent origins of chemical defense. This is a well-established finding in the literature and is supported by Figure 1.

results.result: Prior alkaloid sampling has been biased toward colorful species, with only 31 of 245 inconspicuous species assessed for toxins, and review of prior studies suggests at least 11 undefended species may contain alkaloids.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C46-C47 are supported by systematic review of prior literature documented in Supplementary file 2. The authors provide specific numbers and species identifications, demonstrating clear sampling bias. This contextualizes the novelty of the current study's broader sampling approach.

results.result: The study reveals substantially higher alkaloid diversity in defended species than previously reported, with defended species showing 10-75,000x greater quantities and 10-20x greater diversity than their undefended sister clades, and reports N-methyldecahydroquinolines in new genera.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C69-C75, C87-C91 are supported by comprehensive GC-MS data in Table 1, Figure 2, and Supplementary file 4. The quantitative comparisons between sister clades (e.g., Ameerega vs. Leucostethus, Epipedobates vs. Silverstoneia) are well-documented. The novel detection of N-methyldecahydroquinolines in multiple genera expands knowledge of alkaloid distribution.

results.result: Alkaloids were detected in two bufonid species (Amazophrynella siona, Atelopus aff. spurrelli) but not in Lithodytes lineatus (Leptodactylidae), while Eleutherodactylus cystignathoides showed metabolites assigned to alkaloid pathways, suggesting passive accumulation may have evolved in an older ancestor.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C103 present novel data for non-dendrobatid species, but the sample sizes are very small (1-3 individuals per species) and the UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS data for El. cystignathoides are ambiguous regarding whether detected compounds are true alkaloids or metabolic byproducts. The speculation about ancestral passive accumulation (C103, C110) requires much broader taxonomic sampling to evaluate.

results.result: The authors predict that passive accumulation is the ancestral state in Dendrobatidae and possibly in related taxa, with alkaloid consumption and low resistance preceding the evolution of sequestration mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110, C192 present a phylogenetic hypothesis about ancestral states. While the data showing alkaloids in undefended species support the existence of passive accumulation, formal ancestral state reconstruction is not performed. The hypothesis is plausible given the data but requires explicit phylogenetic analysis and broader taxonomic sampling (especially in Bufonidae, Eleutherodactylidae, Leptodactylidae) to be rigorously tested.

results.result: Different types of toxin resistance (metabolism, target-site modifications) may be important at different evolutionary phases, with common metabolic mechanisms potentially preceding specialized target-site resistance in the evolution of chemical defense.
results.evaluation: Claims C111, C120-C126 are supported by comparative data from multiple toxin-sequestering systems (Karageorgi et al., 2019; Petschenka et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2023; Tarvin et al., 2023). The examples from butterflies, fireflies, and other systems demonstrate that specialized resistance mechanisms are associated with sequestration. The inference about evolutionary sequence is logical but remains a prediction requiring direct testing.

results.result: Prediction 2: Species with passive accumulation have intermediate toxin elimination rates (slower than no accumulation, faster than sequestration). Prediction 3: Sequestration mechanisms are absent in undefended lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C127, C138 are predictions arising from the passive-accumulation hypothesis. These are supported by the experimental data on differential uptake (C128-C137) and sequestration mechanisms (C142-C151). While presented as predictions, the available evidence strongly supports both claims, making them well-founded hypotheses rather than untested predictions.

results.result: The evolution of chemical defenses is constrained by ecological context (tri-trophic interactions, enemy-free space), physiological factors (chemical properties, resistance costs), and may not inevitably occur in all toxin-exposed or toxin-resistant species.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C166 synthesize established ecological and evolutionary theory (Agrawal, 2000; Jeffries and Lawton, 1984) with examples from diverse systems. The discussion of constraints is well-supported by citations and provides important context for understanding why passive accumulation doesn't always lead to sequestration. This represents sound integration of theory with the empirical findings.

results.result: Target-site resistance to toxins often involves trade-offs, with resistance mutations affecting protein function and requiring compensatory mutations, and resistance can carry fitness costs in fecundity, survival, or locomotion.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C173 are well-supported by multiple studies across diverse taxa (Karageorgi et al., 2019; Tarvin et al., 2017; Hague et al., 2018; Kliot and Ghanim, 2012; Züst et al., 2018). The examples demonstrate consistent patterns of resistance costs and compensatory evolution. This contextualizes the evolutionary dynamics of chemical defense evolution.

results.result: Passive accumulation is not a novel concept but has been discussed in contexts of self-medication and bioaccumulation; it may be analogous to organismal functions like vitamin transport and could be widespread in lineages that evolved sequestration.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C186 place the passive accumulation concept in broader context, supported by citations to prior work on self-medication, bioaccumulation, and examples from Drosophila and sawflies showing toxin accumulation without specialized sequestration. The analogies to vitamin transport (C179-C180) are speculative but reasonable. The claim that passive accumulation may be widespread (C186) is plausible but requires more evidence.

results.result: Study limitations include small sample sizes for some species (1-2 individuals), lack of temporal/spatial replication, inability to measure absolute alkaloid quantities due to lack of standards, and inability to detect heavy alkaloids like batrachotoxin and tetrodotoxin with GC-MS.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C190 are acknowledged limitations that are important for interpreting the results. The small sample sizes for some species (Table 1) and lack of standards are genuine constraints. However, the consistency of findings across multiple species and the use of two analytical methods (GC-MS and UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS) provide robustness despite these limitations.

results.result: Background claims establishing the historical context of research on poison frog chemical defenses, the evolution of the diet-toxicity hypothesis, and the application of pharmacokinetic principles to understanding acquired chemical defenses.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C24, C27 provide essential background and are supported by appropriate citations to the primary literature. These establish the historical development of ideas about poison frog chemical defense and introduce the pharmacokinetic framework that motivates the current study. All claims are accurately attributed to cited sources.

results.result: The passive-accumulation hypothesis predicts that phases 3 and 4 may initiate a positive feedback loop intensifying chemical defense over time, and future toxicokinetic studies will shed light on evolutionary steps while providing insights for human therapeutics.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C193-C194 are speculative predictions about future dynamics and applications. The positive feedback loop (C26) is a reasonable prediction but untested. The claims about future research directions (C193) and therapeutic applications (C194) are appropriate forward-looking statements but cannot be evaluated for support from current data.

results.result: The study surveyed 104 animals representing 32 species using GC-MS (89 animals, 30 species) and UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS (15 animals, 2 species), with representation from all major undefended dendrobatid clades.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34, C48-C49 accurately describe the study design and sample composition. The data are presented in Table 1 and Figure 2, showing comprehensive sampling across dendrobatid phylogeny. This represents a substantial expansion of taxonomic coverage compared to prior studies.

results.result: The authors present new GC-MS and UHPLC-HESI-MS/MS data showing that 13 of 14 undefended dendrobatid species contain measurable but low amounts of alkaloids in their skin, contrasting with previous studies that found no or mixed evidence for alkaloids in these species. This includes detection of alkaloids in species from Allobates, Leucostethus, Silverstoneia, and Hyloxalus genera.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly praise these new data as 'high quality,' 'surprising,' and representing 'substantial' expansion of previous investigations. Reviewer 1 states the data are 'of high scientific interest' and provide 'an entirely new perspective.' Reviewer 2 notes the 'important new datasets' and calls the discovery 'important.' No reviewer questions the validity or interpretation of these alkaloid detection results.

results.result: The authors present diet analysis data showing that both defended and undefended dendrobatid species consume substantial proportions of ants and mites (known alkaloid sources), with undefended species consuming high proportions despite not accumulating high alkaloid levels. This suggests that diet alone does not explain the defended phenotype.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states that 'the discovery that changes in diet are not so closely correlated with the presence of alkaloids (based on the expanded sampling of non-defended species) is important, in my opinion.' No reviewer challenges the diet data or the inference that diet is insufficient to explain chemical defense. The data are treated as a significant contribution to understanding the evolution of toxin sequestration.

results.result: The authors propose the 'passive-accumulation hypothesis,' a four-phase evolutionary model for the evolution of chemical defense in poison frogs. This model posits that passive accumulation—temporary toxin retention without derived transport/storage mechanisms—represents an intermediate phenotype between toxin consumption and sequestration, and may be the ancestral state in Dendrobatidae.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 describes the 'suggested scenario' as 'compelling' and states the authors 'have done a fantastic job restructuring the manuscript' to make clear 'which new hypotheses are presented and which testable predictions for future studies derive from these hypotheses.' Reviewer 2 calls this 'a conceptually important paper that provides evidence for the importance of intermediate stages in the evolution of chemical defense and aposematism.' No reviewer challenges the conceptual framework or its plausibility.

results.result: The authors predict that toxin resistance evolves prior to or in concert with passive accumulation and increases with sequestration. They review evidence showing that both defended and undefended frogs can survive alkaloid intake, though resistance mechanisms vary across species and may include target-site resistance, metabolic detoxification, and binding proteins.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this prediction or the supporting evidence from the literature. Reviewer 1 notes the manuscript is 'thorough' in its discussion. The integration of resistance mechanisms into the evolutionary model is treated as a logical component of the hypothesis, with no concerns raised about the interpretation of cited studies or the prediction itself.

results.result: The authors predict that toxin elimination rates differ among phenotypes: slowest in sequestering species, intermediate in passive accumulators, and fastest in non-accumulators. They cite experimental evidence showing undefended frogs accumulate <1% of ingested alkaloids while defended species sequester 10-50%, and note variation in metabolism and elimination even among defended species.
results.evaluation: No reviewer questions this prediction or the cited experimental evidence. The logic connecting elimination rates to the passive-accumulation hypothesis is not challenged. Reviewer 1's statement that the manuscript presents 'testable predictions for future studies' implicitly accepts this as a reasonable prediction arising from the model.

results.result: The authors predict that derived sequestration mechanisms (specialized transport/storage) are absent or minimally expressed in undefended lineages. They review experimental evidence showing undefended species fail to accumulate alkaloids from feeding experiments or accumulate only trace amounts, while defended species show evidence of binding proteins and efficient sequestration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this prediction or the interpretation of experimental evidence. The distinction between passive accumulation and sequestration is central to the model, and no reviewer questions whether this distinction is supported by the cited studies. The prediction is treated as a logical component of the hypothesis.

results.result: The authors report substantially higher alkaloid diversity in defended dendrobatid species than previously documented, including novel findings such as the first report of N-methyldecahydroquinolines outside of five genera. They document hundreds of unique alkaloids in Dendrobatinae and Ameerega/Epipedobates species, with variation in quantity and diversity across species.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praise the 'cutting edge technology' and expanded sampling. Reviewer 1 notes the data 'expands knowledge on major classes of alkaloids within genera.' No concerns are raised about these findings, which are treated as valuable contributions to the field's understanding of alkaloid diversity in defended species.

results.result: The authors detected alkaloids in two bufonid species (Atelopus) and identified alkaloid-pathway metabolites in an eleutherodactylid species. They speculate that passive accumulation may have evolved in an older ancestor shared by Dendrobatidae, Bufonidae, and Eleutherodactylidae, predating convergent origins of sequestration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes that 'although only few non-dendrobatids were included in the alkaloid screening, some of these also included minor quantities of alkaloids, and the capacity of passive alkaloid accumulation may therefore characterize numerous other frog clades, or even amphibians in general.' This indicates acceptance of the data and the broader implications, though the speculation about deep ancestry is acknowledged as tentative.

results.result: The authors discuss broader implications of their model, noting that many animals consume toxins and evolve resistance, and predicting that some may be on evolutionary trajectories toward chemical defense. They discuss ecological and physiological constraints on the evolution of chemical defenses, including costs of resistance, tri-trophic interactions, and co-evolutionary dynamics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'there were some aspects of the paper that I thought could be revised,' specifically requesting 'discussion of the potentially negative effects of toxin accumulation' and 'ecological factors that could impact trajectories of the evolution of toxicity.'
